young.html: Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome about 1,850 years ago. He was the most powerful man in the world. But he did not want to be proud or cruel. Every day he wrote notes to himself in a little notebook: reminders to be fair, patient, kind and calm.

He never meant anyone else to read it. Today we call it the Meditations. In it he tells himself things like: Each morning, expect to meet some grumpy or unkind people. Remember that they are your brothers and sisters, and that we are made to help each other, like two hands.
One of his favorite exercises was to imagine looking down from very high up, so that his worries looked small. Try it below.

young.html: A thank-you list, Marcus style. The first part of the Meditations is a list of people Marcus was grateful to, and what he learned from each: from his grandfather, good manners and a calm temper; from his mother, kindness and simple living. Write your own list: five people, and one good thing you learned from each. You might give one of them a copy.

full.html: Marcus Aurelius (AD 121–180) was adopted, at the emperor Hadrian’s wish, by Hadrian’s successor Antoninus Pius, and became emperor himself in AD 161. As a young man he studied rhetoric with Fronto and philosophy with the Stoic Junius Rusticus. His reign was hard: a plague spread through the empire, and he spent most of his last ten years on campaign against German tribes along the Danube. He died in AD 180, and his son Commodus succeeded him.

The Meditations are twelve short books of notes, written in Greek, mostly in the 170s. The oldest manuscripts call them ta eis heauton, “to himself.” Two of the books carry notes on where they were written: one “among the Quadi at the Granua,” a river on the frontier, and one at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube. They are not a treatise. They are an emperor reminding himself, again and again, how he wants to live.

full.text: Book I: what I learned from others

full.html: Book I is a list of debts: what Marcus learned from his family, teachers and friends. From Rusticus, for instance:

full.text: … to read carefully, and not to be satisfied with a superficial understanding of a book; nor hastily to give my assent to those who talk overmuch; and I am indebted to him for being acquainted with the discourses of Epictetus, which he communicated to me out of his own collection.
full.author: Marcus Aurelius
full.ed: The Chesterfield Society, London and New York
full.note: Long’s translation was first published in 1862.

full.text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil. … I can neither be injured by any of them, for no one can fix on me what is ugly, nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him. For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth.
full.author: Marcus Aurelius
full.ed: The Chesterfield Society, London and New York

full.html: Three Stoic ideas in one paragraph: people do wrong from ignorance of what is good; no one can harm my character but me; and all people are kin, made to work together. Marcus does not pretend difficult people are pleasant. He prepares himself to meet them without anger.

full.text: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself. For nowhere, either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble, does a man retire than into his own soul.
full.author: Marcus Aurelius
full.ed: The Chesterfield Society, London and New York

full.html: Marcus often imagines his life from a great height or across great stretches of time: the whole earth a point, Europe and Asia corners of the universe, the busy people of earlier reigns all gone. The exercise is not meant to make life seem worthless. It shrinks fame, anger and worry down to size, so that what is left (acting justly, now) stands out.

full.html: Reading the Meditations as advice to give up and withdraw. Marcus worked very hard: he judged cases, ran the empire and led armies in his last years. His notes keep turning back to duty: do the work in front of you, as well as you can, for the common good, and do not wait for praise.

items: A rare record: we have almost no other private writing by a Roman emperor. Here a ruler examines his own faults.

The philosopher-king: Plato had hoped that philosophers might rule. Later writers often pointed to Marcus as the nearest example, while noting that he still fought wars, and that he left the throne to a son who ruled badly.
Lasting readers: the Meditations have stayed in print in many languages, and are read today by people from soldiers to students who want a daily practice of self-command.

deep.text: Context: a Stoic on the throne

deep.html: Marcus learned Stoicism largely from Epictetus’s teaching, which he read in Arrian’s notes. Like Epictetus, he believed that a wise reason (which he calls nature, God or the gods) orders the world, that everything changes, and that virtue is the only true good. He writes about these beliefs as his own convictions and also, at times, wonders whether the world is ordered by providence or is only atoms, and concludes that either way he must act justly. His reign also saw the persecution of Christians in some places; how much he himself was responsible is debated by historians.

items: Can a powerful person stay humble? What helped Marcus try?
Is it good to remind yourself often that you will die? Why did Marcus think so?
Marcus says no one can harm your character but you. Is that true, or are we shaped by how others treat us?
Why write notes to yourself? What would you put in your own notebook?

deep.html: Plotinus, the next rung, began teaching in Rome about sixty years after Marcus died, and turned inward in a different way: toward a union of the soul with the One. Augustine’s Confessions is also a book of self-examination, but written as a prayer to God. Montaigne’s essays, later on this ladder, made writing about oneself into a new kind of book.

questions: Marcus expected to meet difficult people each day. How might expecting it help you stay calm?
Who taught you something important? What did they teach you?
Where is your “inner retreat,” the quiet place in your mind you can go to?
When you imagine a problem from very far away, does it look smaller? Does that help, or not?
Marcus was the most powerful man in the world and still wrote reminders to be humble. Why might powerful people need such reminders most?
